meta.title: Why Companies Buy Back Their Own Stock
meta.hook: A company can raise its own stock price without selling a single new product.
meta.description: A stock buyback is a company using its own cash to purchase its own shares on the open market. That shrinks the number of shares outstanding, which raises earnings per remaining share even if total profit stays flat. US public companies collectively spend hundreds of billions of dollars a year on buybacks. Educational content only, not financial advice.

scenes.narration: A company can make its own stock look more valuable without selling one extra product.

visual.visual_intent: A stack of stock certificates under warm light, camera pushing in slowly, cinematic

scenes.narration: It's called a buyback. The company uses its own cash to purchase its own shares.

visual.visual_intent: A glowing financial chart on an office monitor, shares icon shrinking, minimal render

scenes.narration: Buying its own shares off the market shrinks the total number left outstanding.

visual.visual_intent: A donut chart on screen with one segment visibly shrinking, clean data visualization

scenes.narration: Fewer shares means the same total profit gets divided among fewer owners. Each share is worth more of the company.

visual.visual_intent: A pie being divided among fewer plates, each portion visibly larger, simple visual metaphor, cinematic
visual.decision_reason: the causal EPS explanation, kept as a visual metaphor

scenes.narration: It's one reason companies sometimes prefer buybacks over paying out a dividend.

scenes.narration: US public companies collectively spend hundreds of billions of dollars a year buying back their own stock.

scenes.narration: It doesn't create new value out of nothing. It just changes who owns a bigger slice of what's already there. Follow for more.
